name: Apollo 15
short_status: Landed at Hadley-Apennine July 30, 1971; splashed down Aug 7, 1971; its laser retroreflector is still Earth's primary lunar ranging target (as of 2026).
tagline: NASA · United States · Crewed landing · 1971 · The space race Success

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 26 July 1971, 13:34 UTC (9:34 a.m. EDT), Saturn V from Kennedy Space Center Pad 39A

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: David R. Scott (commander), Alfred M. Worden (command module pilot), James B. Irwin (lunar module pilot); CSM Endeavour, LM Falcon

facts.label: Lunar landing
facts.value: 30 July 1971, 22:16:29 UTC at Hadley-Apennine, next to Hadley Rille

facts.label: Surface stay
facts.value: 66 hours 55 minutes, the first three-day lunar surface stay

facts.label: EVAs
facts.value: A 33-minute stand-up EVA by Scott (July 30) plus three surface EVAs of 6h34m (July 31), 7h12m (Aug 1) and 4h50m (Aug 2), totaling 18h37m, a record at the time

facts.label: Lunar Roving Vehicle
facts.value: First LRV drive, 31 July 1971; about 17.5 miles (roughly 28 km) driven across three traverses, hitting 12 km/h

facts.label: Samples returned
facts.value: About 170 lb (77 kg) of rock and soil, including a core from about 10 feet down

facts.label: Genesis Rock
facts.value: Sample 15415, an anorthosite about 4 billion years old, collected 1 Aug 1971 at Spur crater (Station 7)

facts.label: Laser retroreflector
facts.value: 105 x 65 cm array, the largest of the four working arrays on the Moon and still the primary target for lunar laser ranging; distances measured to centimeter level or better (page updated 23 Sep 2025)

facts.label: LM liftoff
facts.value: 2 Aug 1971; the first lunar liftoff seen live on Earth, televised by the LRV camera parked about 500 feet away

facts.label: Subsatellite
facts.value: 80-lb Particles and Fields Subsatellite released on the 74th and final lunar orbit (4 Aug 1971), the first satellite launched from a crewed spacecraft

facts.label: Deep-space EVA
facts.value: 5 Aug 1971: Worden's 39-minute spacewalk to retrieve SIM-bay film about 200,000 miles from Earth, the first EVA in cislunar space

facts.label: Splashdown
facts.value: 7 Aug 1971, about 4:46 p.m. EDT in the Pacific about 335 miles north of Honolulu, recovered by USS Okinawa; one of three main chutes collapsed but the system was designed to land safely on two

facts.label: Mission duration
facts.value: 12 days 7 hours (about 295 hours), the longest crewed lunar mission to that date

facts.label: Modern successor
facts.value: NGLR-1, a next-generation retroreflector designed to improve on the Apollo arrays with sub-millimeter ranging, landed at Mare Crisium on Firefly's Blue Ghost, 2 March 2025

timeline: Launch from Kennedy Space Center Pad 39A at 13:34 UTC
Falcon lands at Hadley-Apennine at 22:16:29 UTC; Scott surveys the site in a 33-minute stand-up EVA through the top hatch
EVA-1 (6h34m): first drive of the Lunar Roving Vehicle, to Elbow crater and the Apennine Front; ALSEP and laser retroreflector deployed
EVA-2 (7h12m): Genesis Rock (sample 15415) found at Spur crater, Station 7
EVA-3 (4h50m) to Hadley Rille; Scott's hammer-and-feather drop; liftoff televised for the first time via the LRV camera
Subsatellite released on the 74th lunar orbit; trans-Earth injection burn (2m21s)
Worden performs the first deep-space EVA, 39 minutes about 200,000 miles from Earth
Splashdown in the Pacific on two of three main parachutes; crew recovered by USS Okinawa
LRO rolls east to shoot the definitive oblique of the landing site, Hadley Rille and the astronauts' tracks
NASA reiterates the Apollo 15 retroreflector is the primary lunar laser ranging target, with ranges routine at centimeter level or better
